A content delivery network solves a simple problem: a website's true home, called the origin server, might sit far away, so every visitor waits for data to travel a long distance. To fix this, copies of the site's content get stored on many machines scattered around the world, each called an edge location, positioned closer to where people actually are. When a request arrives and the nearby copy already has what's needed, that's called a cache hit, meaning the answer comes back almost instantly instead of making the long trip back to the origin. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries stocking popular books so nobody has to travel to the one central library across the country every time they want to read something. If the nearby location doesn't have a fresh copy, it quietly fetches one from the origin, stores it, and serves it faster to everyone else after that. This system keeps websites, videos, and apps loading quickly regardless of location, spreads the workload so no single server gets overwhelmed, and adds resilience since traffic can shift between locations if one has trouble. Streaming services, online stores, and news sites all rely on this arrangement to feel fast and reliable everywhere at once.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing the real, complete version of a website | Everything ultimately traces back to it when nothing closer has the answer |
| Edge location | A nearby storage point holding copies of popular content | Shortens the distance data has to travel, speeding things up |
| Cache hit | A successful case where the nearby copy already has what's needed | Delivers instant results without contacting the distant origin |
| Latency | The delay between asking for something and receiving it | Lower delay means smoother browsing, video, and app experiences |
